Name: obligatory_marking_scaffold
Title: Grammar as a Cognitive Forcing Function: Do Obligatorily-Marked Grammatical Categories Scaffold LLM Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in which information they OBLIGATORILY encode in grammar (evidentiality/source, definiteness, number, gender, tense/aspect). We hypothesize that forcing an LLM to reason in a language whose grammar obligatorily marks a task-relevant dimension causally improves reasoning on that dimension—because the grammar acts as a 'thinking-for-speaking' forcing function that hard-wires attention to information the model would otherwise drop—whereas reasoning in a language that leaves that dimension optional yields more errors. This isolates a precise, causal, feature-specific mechanism by which language shapes machine intelligence, beyond aggregate data or typology effects.
Related Work: Cognitive science ('thinking for speaking', Slobin; Boroditsky on grammatical gender/number effects on human categorization) motivates that obligatory grammatical marking directs attention. In LLMs, prior work studies (a) multilingual reasoning gaps attributed to data quantity (MGSM, cross-lingual CoT), (b) broad typology-accuracy correlations, and (c) linguistic inductive biases in spatial/navigation prompting (Zhang et al. 2026) and cross-linguistic moral divergence under ambiguity (Powdthavee 2026). None isolate the causal effect of a SPECIFIC obligatory grammatical category on reasoning about the exact dimension that category encodes, nor test the matched prediction that marking helps ONLY when the marked dimension is task-relevant (a double dissociation). Unlike my prior typology proposal (broad features predicting accuracy) this targets a single mechanism—obligatory vs optional marking as a reasoning scaffold—with a tightly controlled feature-times-task design and an intervention that inserts/removes obligatory marking.
Abstract: Every language forces its speakers to encode certain information: some obligatorily mark the source of a claim (evidentiality), others obligatorily mark definiteness, number, or gender, while other languages leave these optional. Cognitive science suggests such obligatory marking is a 'thinking-for-speaking' forcing function that directs attention to the marked dimension. We ask whether the same holds for large language models: does reasoning in a language that obligatorily marks a task-relevant dimension causally improve reasoning about that dimension? We design reasoning tasks each keyed to a specific grammatical dimension—evidential/source-tracking (who said what, hearsay vs. direct evidence), quantity/number reasoning, definiteness/reference tracking, and gender/entity disambiguation. For each dimension we select languages that obligatorily mark it (e.g., Turkish/Quechua evidentiality, languages with obligatory dual/plural, obligatory articles, obligatory gender) versus matched languages that leave it optional, verifying content equivalence via back-translation and controlling training-data frequency in mixed-effects regression. The key prediction is a DOUBLE DISSOCIATION: obligatory marking helps only when the marked dimension is task-relevant, not across the board. We further run a causal intervention: programmatically INSERT explicit marking (or STRIP it) into otherwise identical prompts within a single language, to isolate the marking effect from all cross-language confounds. We evaluate open multilingual models (Qwen2.5, Aya, Llama-3, Gemma-2). Results would show that specific grammatical categories act as targeted cognitive scaffolds in LLMs, reframing part of machine reasoning as a product of the information a language forces one to track, with implications for prompt design and language–thought theories.
Experiments: 1) DIMENSION-KEYED TASK SUITES (~150 problems each) targeting four grammatical dimensions: (a) EVIDENTIALITY/source-tracking—short narratives where the answer depends on whether a fact was directly witnessed, inferred, or hearsay; (b) NUMBER—quantity/counting and singular/dual/plural distinctions that determine the answer; (c) DEFINITENESS/reference—multi-sentence discourse where tracking which referent is 'the known one' vs 'a new one' determines the answer; (d) GENDER—pronoun/antecedent disambiguation resolvable via gender marking. Each problem has a verifier and a control variant where the marked dimension is irrelevant. 2) LANGUAGE SELECTION: for each dimension pick 2–3 languages that OBLIGATORILY mark it and 2–3 matched languages that leave it OPTIONAL, spanning resource levels; render all tasks into all languages, verifying semantic equivalence via round-trip translation and spot human checks. 3) CROSS-LANGUAGE MAIN TEST: for each open model (Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B), prompt to reason and answer in each language; fit mixed-effects logistic regression: correct ~ obligatory_marking(dim) * task_relevance + log(data_freq) + (1|problem) + (1|model). The critical coefficient is the marking*relevance interaction (predicted positive)—the DOUBLE DISSOCIATION that marking helps only when the dimension matters. 4) WITHIN-LANGUAGE CAUSAL INTERVENTION (removes cross-language confounds): in a single language that allows optional marking, generate matched prompts that either INSERT explicit marking of the task-relevant dimension (e.g., add evidential particles / explicit articles / explicit number) or STRIP it, holding all else fixed; measure accuracy delta. Reverse intervention: strip obligatory marking (where grammatically degradable) and measure degradation. 5) MECHANISM: with CoT, measure whether marked-dimension information appears/persists in the reasoning trace more often under obligatory/inserted marking (trace-mention rate), and test mediation (marking → trace-mention → correctness). 6) GENERALIZATION: check the interaction holds across all four dimensions and models; report per-dimension effect sizes. METRICS: accuracy, marking*relevance interaction coefficient and effect size, within-language insertion/stripping accuracy delta, trace-mention rate, mediation effect; all with mixed-effects models and CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Cross-language comparisons are confounded by data quantity/quality and lexical differences; mitigated by data-frequency covariates, matched-content design, and—crucially—the within-language insertion/stripping intervention that removes cross-language confounds. 2) Obligatory grammatical categories co-vary with other typological features; the double-dissociation design (marking helps only when relevant) guards against generic 'this language is just better' explanations. 3) Programmatic insertion/stripping of marking may produce slightly disfluent text; we validate fluency and semantic equivalence with automated checks and human spot-checks. 4) Some dimensions cannot be cleanly stripped in obligatorily-marking languages; we focus stripping tests where grammatically feasible and rely on insertion tests elsewhere. 5) Effects may be small or model-specific; multiple models and effect-size reporting address this. 6) Translation may leak the answer via the marked feature even in 'optional' languages if translators over-specify; we control translations to keep optional marking optional and audit a sample. 7) A null interaction would still be informative, indicating obligatory grammar does not function as a reasoning scaffold in current LLMs.
